queue.title: Auditor Independence Matters More Than Reporting Speed
queue.content:
Pressure to release financial reports faster rarely justifies weakening audit independence. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

Pressure to release a financial report earlier rarely justifies concessions in the depth and independence of the audit process.

Pressure to release a financial report earlier rarely justifies concessions in the depth and independence of the audit process.

When the market or investors push for faster disclosure of financial results, there's constant pressure to shorten the audit process — which can, over the long run, undermine the very trust that publishing the results was meant to build.

Organisations that clearly communicate that audit independence and thoroughness take priority over speed of release generally build a more stable relationship with long-term investors than those who treat speed as a virtue in itself.

This commentary is part of the GNK ASG Intelligence Desk system and is informational in nature.

queue.title: Managing Supplier Quality Through Systematic KPI Tracking
queue.content:
A supplier's quality rarely collapses overnight — systematic KPI tracking catches the decline before it reaches the customer. A publication by Nermin Sefić.

A supplier's quality rarely collapses overnight — the decline is visible in the data long before it reaches the end customer.

A supplier's quality rarely collapses overnight — the pattern of gradual decline is visible in the data long before it becomes a visible problem for the end customer.

Delivery quality from a given supplier rarely worsens suddenly — a gradual decline pattern, visible through indicators like on-time delivery rate and claim rate, precedes any problem visible to the end customer.

Systematically tracking key performance indicators (KPIs) for every critical supplier, rather than relying on a subjective sense of the relationship, allows for early intervention before problems escalate.

A regular quarterly review of results with the supplier, grounded in agreed, measurable indicators, turns relationship management from reactive firefighting into proactive collaboration.

Clearly defined thresholds that trigger a formal improvement plan or a search for alternatives prevent a declining supplier relationship from dragging on longer than is justified.

queue.title: Managing Flexible Work Models and Productivity
queue.content:
Measuring hybrid-work productivity by online hours instead of output creates a needless conflict. A publication by Nermin Sefić.

Measuring productivity by hours spent online instead of by actual output creates a conflict in hybrid models that doesn't have to exist.

Measuring productivity by hours spent online instead of by actual output creates a conflict in hybrid models that doesn't have to exist.

The shift to hybrid and remote work models revealed that many organisations lacked clear performance indicators independent of physical presence, so they reached for activity tracking as a proxy instead.

Tracking hours logged into the system, instead of actual task completion and results achieved, creates a culture of visible busyness that doesn't reflect real productivity.

Defining clear, measurable goals per role, regardless of whether an employee works from the office or from home, allows for a fairer and more accurate assessment of contribution than presence tracking does.

Flexibility in the work model and clear accountability for results are not opposing goals — organisations that successfully combine both build trust, rather than surveillance, as the basis of the employee relationship.

queue.title: Managing International Customs Risk
queue.content:
A sudden customs policy shift can change an export-import line's profitability overnight. A publication by Nermin Sefić.

A sudden change in customs policy can change the profitability of an entire export-import business line overnight.

A sudden change in customs policy can change the profitability of an entire export-import business line overnight.

Companies engaged in international trade increasingly face rapid shifts in customs policy that can directly and significantly affect the profitability of individual product lines almost overnight.

Tracking the announcement and likelihood of trade-policy changes in key markets, rather than reacting only after they take effect, buys time to adjust pricing strategy or the supply chain.

Diversifying sourcing and sales markets across multiple customs jurisdictions reduces a business's sensitivity to a policy change in any single country or trade bloc.

Scenario planning the margin impact of different customs outcomes, done in advance, enables faster decisions on price or supply-chain adjustments once a change actually happens.

queue.title: Investor Relations Through Regular Communication
queue.content:
An investor who only hears bad news builds weaker trust than one informed on a regular rhythm. A publication by Nermin Sefić.

An investor who only hears from a company when something goes wrong builds a different kind of trust than one who is kept regularly informed.

An investor who only hears from a company when something goes wrong builds a different kind of trust than one who is kept regularly informed.

A regular, pre-announced rhythm of investor communication — quarterly reports, an annual review — builds predictability that reduces the need for anxious questions between those dates.

Investors who receive the same information regardless of whether the quarter was good or bad develop trust in the consistency of communication, not just in current results.

Proactively communicating challenges before an investor discovers them independently builds credibility over the long run, even when it means admitting worse news in the short term.

A structured channel for investor questions, with a clear response deadline, prevents individual investors from receiving different levels of information depending on personal ties to management.

queue.title: Securing Industrial Control Systems (OT)
queue.content:
OT security needs a different approach than standard IT — an attack on industrial control systems has physical consequences. A publication by Nermin Sefić.

Operational technology that controls physical processes requires a different security approach than standard IT, because an attack here has physical consequences.

Operational technology (OT) that controls physical processes requires a different security approach than standard IT systems, because an attack here has physical consequences.

Systems that control physical industrial processes — production lines, energy plants — are increasingly connected to the IT network for analytics and remote monitoring, and in the process inherit its security risks.

Unlike an IT security incident, which usually means data loss, compromising an industrial control system can have direct physical consequences for equipment, worker safety, and the environment.

Network segmentation that separates operational technology from the standard business IT network, with strict control of connection points, remains a key but often insufficiently applied protective measure.

A security team responsible for OT systems needs to understand industrial processes, not just standard IT security, because measures acceptable in an office environment can compromise the safety of a production process.
